---
title: "Level segments"
description: "How OPDI finds periods of level flight, cruise included (level-start and level-end)."
---

## In one sentence

`level-start` and `level-end` mark the start and the end of each period in
which the aircraft flies level, cruise included.

## What it needs

- The cleaned barometric altitude, vertical rate and ground speed of the
  track's reports (see [Cleaning of position reports](cleaning.qmd)), with the
  same plausibility limits as the [tops](tops.qmd).
- The elevation of the departure and destination airports, to tell flight
  from the ground.

## How it is computed

### Flight phases (`level-start`, `level-end`)

1. **Phase of each report.** Each report is given one of five phases by
   **fuzzy logic**: each phase has a rule that scores, between 0 and 1, how
   well the report fits it on three inputs, and keeps the lowest of the three
   scores. A rule is used only when all three inputs are known.

   | Phase | Altitude | Vertical rate | Ground speed |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | Ground | near the airport (score 0 from 200 ft above it) | near 0 ft/min | near 0 kt |
   | Climb | around 10,000 ft (wide) | climbing (full score from 1,000 ft/min) | around 300 kt |
   | Descent | around 10,000 ft (wide) | descending (full score from 1,000 ft/min) | around 300 kt |
   | Cruise | around 35,000 ft (wide) | near 0 ft/min | around 600 kt |
   | Level | around 10,000 ft (wide) | near 0 ft/min | around 300 kt |

   The phase with the highest score wins. The ground membership is measured
   from the lower of the heights above the departure and destination
   airports.
2. **Smoothing.** Each report takes the phase that is most common within 30 s
   before and after it (a 60 s window), which removes single misclassified
   reports.
3. **Events.** `level-start` is placed at a report in cruise or level flight
   whose previous report had another phase, and `level-end` at a report in
   cruise or level flight whose next report has another phase.
4. **Checks.** A segment shorter than 20 s (a single report, for instance) is
   not published. A report flagged on the ground, or less than 200 ft above
   the departure or destination airport, is never level flight, so there are
   no level segments on the ground or on the take-off or landing roll.

### Level segments of the vertical flight efficiency method {#pru-level-segments}

The tops and the [level-offs](level-offs.qmd) use a second, geometric
definition of level flight. These segments are not published as events of
their own.

1. Interpolate the altitude in a straight line onto a grid of one point every
   10 s, only between the first and the last measured altitude of each piece
   of the track.
2. A grid point is **level** when the altitude stays within a band of 50 ft
   over the next 10 s (a vertical speed of at most 300 ft/min). A point that
   lies between two measured altitudes more than 60 s apart is not level: the
   altitude there was not measured.
3. Consecutive level points form a segment, which ends 10 s after its last
   level point. Its altitude is its mean altitude. Segments shorter than 20 s
   are dropped.

Nothing is computed across a reception gap of more than 30 minutes kept
inside a track: each piece is handled on its own.

## Based on

- **Flight phases**: the fuzzy-logic phase identification of
  [Sun, Ellerbroek and Hoekstra (2017)](../resources.qmd#ref-sun-2017), with the rules and
  membership values of its code in [OpenAP](../resources.qmd#ref-sun-2020). OpenAP labels
  60 s windows from the mean altitude, speed and vertical rate of each window;
  OPDI labels each report and then takes the most common phase within 60 s.
  The use of complete rules only, the ground height above the airports and
  the checks of step 4 were added for OPDI.
- **Geometric level segments**: the rolling window of the vertical flight
  efficiency method of the EUROCONTROL Performance Review Unit
  ([Peeters and Guastalla, 2017](../resources.qmd#ref-pru-vfe)): a window of 10 s and 50 ft
  (300 ft/min) over altitudes interpolated in a straight line. The shortest
  segment, 20 s, is the minimum level time of ICAO's KPI17 and KPI19
  ([GANP KPI overview](../resources.qmd#ref-ganp-kpi)).

## What is published

Event types `level-start` and `level-end`, with position, altitude,
`distance_flown_nm` and `time_passed_s`. Their `info` is empty.

## Use cases

- **Time and distance in cruise**: pairs of `level-start` and `level-end` at
  the highest altitude of the flight.
- **Step climbs**: several level segments at increasing altitudes in cruise.
- **Level flight at low altitude** around an airport, from segments below
  `top-of-climb` or after `top-of-descent`.

## Limitations

The phases of slow aircraft (turboprops, light aircraft) are less reliable,
because the cruise rule centres on 600 kt; a light aircraft's cruise can split
into many segments. See
[Limitations: vertical profile](../limitations.qmd#lim-vertical).
